title: Statement and Coordinate Setup
content:
The British Flag theorem states that for a rectangle ABCD and any point P in its plane, PA² + PC² = PB² + PD², where A,C and B,D are the two pairs of opposite corners. The name comes from the Union-Jack-like figure formed by the segments from P to the four corners.

The formalization works in coordinates over ℝ × ℝ. Rather than place the rectangle in a fixed position, we encode 'rectangle' intrinsically by two algebraic conditions on the vertices: a parallelogram closure C = B + D − A (the quadrilateral closes up), and a right angle at A, expressed as the orthogonality of the edge vectors B − A and D − A.
mathContext: Rectangle conditions: $C = B + D - A$ and $(B - A) \cdot (D - A) = 0$. Claim: $PA^2 + PC^2 = PB^2 + PD^2$ for all $P$.

title: Squared Distance
content: `sqDist P Q` is the squared Euclidean distance (P.1 − Q.1)² + (P.2 − Q.2)² between two planar points. Working with squared distances rather than distances is what makes the proof a pure polynomial identity: no `Real.sqrt` appears, so the whole result is closed by ring arithmetic over ℝ.

title: The British Flag Identity
content:
The core theorem `british_flag`. After substituting the parallelogram closure C = B + D − A, the goal expands to a polynomial identity in the coordinates. Writing u = B − A and v = D − A, the key cancellation is

(PA² + PC²) − (PB² + PD²) = 2 (u.1·v.1 + u.2·v.2) = 2 (u ⬝ v).

The right-hand side is exactly twice the orthogonality hypothesis, so a single `linear_combination (2 : ℝ) * hperp` closes the goal. The theorem is therefore a metric restatement of the right angle at A: the squared-distance identity holds precisely because the edges are perpendicular.
mathContext: $(PA^2+PC^2)-(PB^2+PD^2) = 2(u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2)$ with $u = B-A$, $v = D-A$; this vanishes by $u \cdot v = 0$.
